title: Electron Temperature and Electron-Electron Scattering Length in GaAs/AlGaAs Using Mesoscopic Multiparallel Aperture Geometries
authors: Arati Thapa, Rishav Khatiwada, Prakash Sharma, Jean J. Heremans, Adbhut Gupta, Kirk W. Baldwin, Loren N. Pfeiffer, Mansour Shayegan
abstract: Quantifying electron temperatures and electron-electron scattering lengths is essential for understanding electron transport regimes in two-dimensional systems. To that end, this work experimentally investigates low-temperature ballistic transport using semiclassical cyclotron orbits in a multiparallel aperture geometry. The mesoscopic geometry is fabricated on a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure of very high electron mobility. The amplitudes of maxima in magnetoresistance due to ballistic transport are observed to decay exponentially with temperature, allowing determination of the electron-electron scattering length from the data. A quantitative relation between electron temperature and an applied dc bias heating current is established by comparing magnetoresistance peak amplitudes measured as a function of temperature and dc bias, reflecting bias-induced Joule heating. In addition, the resistance measured near zero magnetic field decreases with increasing temperature, providing signatures of superballistic conductance.
summary: The research experimentally investigates electron temperature and electron-electron scattering length in high-mobility GaAs/AlGaAs 2DES using a mesoscopic aperture geometry. By measuring magnetoresistance oscillations as a function of temperature and applied bias current, the authors successfully determined the electron-electron scattering length and quantified how Joule heating elevates the electron temperature above the lattice temperature.
main_problem: The study aims to quantify electron temperatures ($T_e$) and the electron-electron scattering length ($\ell_{ee}$) in two-dimensional electron systems (2DES) under non-equilibrium conditions.
main_result: The authors established a method to determine $\ell_{ee}$ by analyzing the exponential decay of magnetoresistance peaks with temperature, and they quantified $T_e$ via its quadratic dependence on applied DC bias current ($I_{DC}$).
method: Experimental measurements were performed using low-temperature ballistic transport in a mesoscopic multiparallel aperture geometry fabricated on GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures.
model_or_system: The physical system is a high-mobility 2DES confined in a perforated barrier structure. The analysis uses semiclassical cyclotron orbits and models the magnetoresistance amplitude decay based on electron-electron scattering theory.
key_observables: Magnetoresistance $R(B)$ peaks, which are analyzed for their amplitude dependence on temperature ($T$) and DC bias current ($I_{DC}$); also measured is $R(B=0)$ vs $T$.
important_parameters: Electron temperature ($T_e$), electron-electron scattering length ($\ell_{ee}$), cyclotron orbit diameter, and the applied DC heating current ($I_{DC}$).
main_assumptions:
The amplitude of magnetoresistance maxima is assumed to correlate with the number of electrons reaching the collector; non-equilibrium heating implies $T_e > T$ when $I_{DC} 
eq 0$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mesoscopic geometry and cyclotron orbits, showing how magnetoresistance peaks vary with temperature. Other figures plot measured amplitudes vs $T$, fitting these to extract $\ell_{ee}(T)$, and show $R(B=0)$ vs $T$ to identify superballistic conductance regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the necessity of quantifying $T_e$ and $\ell_{ee}$ in 2DES, detailing the measurement technique using mesoscopic apertures, deriving relationships between peak amplitudes and scattering lengths, and finally applying this framework to study temperature dependence via both thermal cooling and bias-induced Joule heating.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controlled experimental platform for studying non-equilibrium electron dynamics in low dimensions. The ability to deterministically control $T_e$ via current injection allows for the direct measurement of scattering mechanisms, which is crucial for understanding energy relaxation in quantum devices.
